entries.c6ebf64da2a96eda7f4f54774ec56cff8b4cbdc4: <div sID="gen18605" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="Ezek.12" sID="Ezek.12"/> <div eID="gen18605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18606" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18607" type="x-p"/> Though the vision of God's glory had gone up from the prophet, yet his word comes to him still, and is by him sent to the people, and to the same purport with that which was discovered to him in the vision, namely, to set forth the terrible judgments that were coming upon Jerusalem, by which the city and temple should be entirely laid waste. In this chapter, I. The prophet, by removing his stuff, and quitting his lodgings, must be a sign to set forth Zedekiah's flight out of Jerusalem in the utmost confusion when the Chaldeans took the city, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.1-Ezek.12.16">ver. 1-16</reference>. II. The prophet, by eating his meat with trembling, must be a sign to set forth the famine in the city during the siege, and the consternation that the inhabitants should be in, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.17-Ezek.12.20">ver. 17-20</reference>. III. A message is sent from God to the people, to assure them that all these predictions should have their accomplishment very shortly, and not be deferred, as they flattered themselves they would be, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.21-Ezek.12.28">ver. 21-28</reference>.
entries.f855f32543ebc0fc5b05e1f342d1391543df12ee: <div eID="gen18607" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18606" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Zedekiah's Captivity Foretold. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 593.)</title> <div sID="gen18608" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> also came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Son of man, thou dwellest in the midst of a rebellious house, which have eyes to see, and see not; they have ears to hear, and hear not: for they <hi type="italic">are</hi> a rebellious house. <hi type="super">3</hi> Therefore, thou son of man, prepare thee stuff for removing, and remove by day in their sight; and thou shalt remove from thy place to another place in their sight: it may be they will consider, though they <hi type="italic">be</hi> a rebellious house. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then shalt thou bring forth thy stuff by day in their sight, as stuff for removing: and thou shalt go forth at even in their sight, as they that go forth into captivity. <hi type="super">5</hi> Dig thou through the wall in their sight, and carry out thereby. <hi type="super">6</hi> In their sight shalt thou bear <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon <hi type="italic">thy</hi> shoulders, <hi type="italic">and</hi> carry <hi type="italic">it</hi> forth in the twilight: thou shalt cover thy face, that thou see not the ground: for I have set thee <hi type="italic">for</hi> a sign unto the house of Israel. <hi type="super">7</hi> And I did so as I was commanded: I brought forth my stuff by day, as stuff for captivity, and in the even I digged through the wall with mine hand; I brought <hi type="italic">it</hi> forth in the twilight, <hi type="italic">and</hi> I bare <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon <hi type="italic">my</hi> shoulder in their sight. <hi type="super">8</hi> And in the morning came the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto me, saying, <hi type="super">9</hi> Son of man, hath not the house of Israel, the rebellious house, said unto thee, What doest thou? <hi type="super">10</hi> Say thou unto them, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; This burden <hi type="italic">concerneth</hi> the prince in Jerusalem, and all the house of Israel that <hi type="italic">are</hi> among them. <hi type="super">11</hi> Say, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> your sign: like as I have done, so shall it be done unto them: they shall remove <hi type="italic">and</hi> go into captivity. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the prince that <hi type="italic">is</hi> among them shall bear upon <hi type="italic">his</hi> shoulder in the twilight, and shall go forth: they shall dig through the wall to carry out thereby: he shall cover his face, that he see not the ground with <hi type="italic">his</hi> eyes. <hi type="super">13</hi> My net also will I spread upon him, and he shall be taken in my snare: and I will bring him to Babylon <hi type="italic">to</hi> the land of the Chaldeans; yet shall he not see it, though he shall die there. <hi type="super">14</hi> And I will scatter toward every wind all that <hi type="italic">are</hi> about him to help him, and all his bands; and I will draw out the sword after them. <hi type="super">15</hi> And they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , when I shall scatter them among the nations, and disperse them in the countries. <hi type="super">16</hi> But I will leave a few men of them from the sword, from the famine, and from the pestilence; that they may declare all their abominations among the heathen whither they come; and they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen18608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18609" type="x-p"/> Perhaps Ezekiel reflected with so much pleasure upon the vision he had had of the glory of God that often, since it went up from him, he was wishing it might come down to him again, and, having seen it once and a second time, he was willing to hope he might be a third time so favoured; but we do not find that he ever saw it any more, and yet <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord comes to</hi> him; for God did <hi type="italic">in divers manners speak to the fathers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.1">Heb. i. 1</reference>) and they often <hi type="italic">heard the words of God</hi> when they did not <hi type="italic">see the visions of the Almighty.</hi> Faith comes by hearing that word of prophecy which is more sure than vision. We may keep up our communion with God without raptures and ecstasies. In these verses the prophet is directed, <div eID="gen18609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18610" type="x-p"/> I. By what signs and actions to express the approaching captivity of Zedekiah king of Judah; that was the thing to be foretold, and it is foretold to those that are already in captivity, because as long as Zedekiah was upon the throne they flattered themselves with hopes that he would make his part good with the king of Babylon, whose yoke he was now projecting to shake off, from which, it is probable, these poor captives promised themselves great things; and it may be, when he was forming that design, he privately sent encouragement to them to hope that he would rescue them shortly, or procure their liberty by exchange of prisoners. While they were fed with these vain hopes they could not set themselves either to submit to their affliction or to get good by their affliction. It was therefore necessary, but very difficult, to convince them that Zedekiah, instead of being their deliverer, should very shortly be their fellow-suffered. Now, one would think it might have been sufficient if the prophet had only told them this in God's name, as he does afterwards (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.10">v. 10</reference>); but, to prepare them for the prophecy of it, he must first give them a sign of it, must speak it to their eyes first and then to their ears: and here we have, 1. The reason why he must take this method (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.2">v. 2</reference>): It is because they are a stupid, dull, unthinking people, that will not heed or will soon forget what they only hear of, or at least will not be at all affected with it; it will make no impression at all upon them: <hi type="italic">Thou dwellest in the midst of a rebellious house,</hi> whom it is next to impossible to work any good upon. <hi type="italic">They have eyes and ears,</hi> they have intellectual powers and faculties, but they <hi type="italic">see not,</hi> they <hi type="italic">hear not.</hi> They were idolaters, whose character it was that they were like the idols they worshipped, which <hi type="italic">have eyes and see not, ears and hear not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.115.5-Ps.115.6">Ps. cxv. 5, 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.8">8</reference>. Note, Those are to be reckoned rebellious that shut their eyes against the divine light and stop their ears to the divine law. The ignorance of those that are wilfully ignorant, that have faculties and means and will not use them, is so far from being their excuse that it adds rebellion to their sin. None so blind, so deaf, as those that will not see, that will not hear. They <hi type="italic">see not,</hi> they <hi type="italic">hear not; for they are a rebellious house.</hi> The cause is all from themselves: the darkness of the understanding is owing to the stubbornness of the will. Now this is the reason why he must speak to them by signs, as deaf people are taught, that they might be either instructed or ashamed. Note, Ministers must accommodate themselves not only to the weakness, but to the wilfulness of those they deal with, and deal with them accordingly: if they dwell among those that are rebellious they must speak to them the more plainly and pressingly, and take that course that is most likely to work upon them, that they may be left inexcusable. 2. The method he just took to awaken and affect them; he must furnish himself with all necessaries <hi type="italic">for removing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.3">v. 3</reference>), provide for a journey clothes and money; he must <hi type="italic">remove from one place to another,</hi> as one unsettled and forced to shift; this he must do <hi type="italic">by day, in the sight</hi> of the people; he must bring out all his household goods, to be packed up and sent away (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.4">v. 4</reference>); and, because all the doors and gates were either locked up that they could not pass through them or so guarded by the enemy that they durst not, he must therefore <hi type="italic">dig through the wall,</hi> and convey his goods away clandestinely through that breach in the wall, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.5">v. 5</reference>. He must carry his goods away himself upon his own shoulders, for want of a servant to attend him; he must do this <hi type="italic">in the twilight,</hi> that he might not be discovered; and, when he has made what shift he can to secure some of the best of his effects, he must himself steal away <hi type="italic">at evening in their sight,</hi> with fear and trembling, and must go <hi type="italic">as those that go forth into captivity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.4">v. 4</reference>); that is, he must <hi type="italic">cover</hi> his <hi type="italic">face</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.6">v. 6</reference>) as being ashamed to be seen and afraid to be known, or in token of very great sorrow and concern; he must go away as a poor broken tradesman, who, when he is forced to shut up shop, hides his head, or quits his country. Thus Ezekiel must be himself a sign to them; and when perhaps he seemed somewhat backward to put himself to all this trouble, and to expose himself to be bantered and ridiculed for it, to reconcile him to it God says (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.3">v. 3</reference>) "<hi type="italic">It may be they will consider,</hi> and will by it be taken off from their vain confidence, <hi type="italic">though they be a rebellious house.</hi>" Note, We must not despair even of the worst, but that yet they may be brought to bethink themselves and repent; and therefore we must continue the use of proper means for their conviction and conversion, because, while there is life, there is hope. And ministers must be willing to go through the most difficult and inconvenient offices (for such was this of Ezekiel's removing), though there be but the <hi type="italic">it may be</hi> of success. If but one soul be awakened to consider, our care and pains will be well bestowed. 3. Ezekiel's ready and punctual obedience to the orders God gave him (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">I did so as I was commanded.</hi> Hereby he teaches us all, and ministers especially, (1.) To obey with cheerfulness every command of God, even the most difficult. Christ himself <hi type="italic">learned obedience,</hi> and so we must all. (2.) To do all we can for the good of the souls of others, to put ourselves to any trouble or pains for the conviction of those that are unconvinced. <hi type="italic">We do all things</hi> (that is, we are willing to do any thing), <hi type="italic">dearly beloved, for your edifying.</hi> (3.) To be ourselves affected with those things wherewith we desire to affect others. When Ezekiel would give his hearers a melancholy prospect he does himself put on a melancholy aspect. (4.) To sit loose to this world, and prepare to leave it, to carry out our <hi type="italic">stuff for removing,</hi> because <hi type="italic">we have here no continuing city. Arise, depart, this it not your rest, for it is polluted.</hi> Thou dwellest <hi type="italic">in a rebellious house,</hi> therefore prepare for removing; for who would not be willing to leave such a house, such a wicked world as this is? <div eID="gen18610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18611" type="x-p"/> II. He is directed by what words to explain those signs and actions, as Agabus, when he bound his own hands and feet, told whose binding was thereby signified. But observe, It was not till morning that God gave him an exposition of the sign, till the next morning, to keep up in him a continual dependence upon God for instruction. As what God does, so what he directs us to do, perhaps we know not now, but shall know hereafter. <div eID="gen18611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18612" type="x-p"/> 1. It was supposed that the people would ask the meaning of this sign, or at least they should (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Hath not the house of Israel said unto thee, What doest thou?</hi> Yes, I know they have. <hi type="italic">Though they</hi> are <hi type="italic">a rebellious house,</hi> yet they are inquisitive concerning the mind of God," as those (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.2">Isa. lviii. 2</reference>) who <hi type="italic">sought God daily. Therefore</hi> the prophet must do such a strange uncouth thing, that they might enquire what it meant; and then, it may be hoped, people will take notice of what is told them, and profit by it, when it comes to them in answer to their enquiries. But some understand it as an intimation that they had not made any such enquiries: "<hi type="italic">Hath not this rebellious house</hi> so much as asked thee, <hi type="italic">What doest thou?</hi> No; they take no notice of it; but tell them the meaning of it, though they do not ask." Note, When God sends to us by his ministers he observes what entertainment we give to the messages he sends us; he hearkens and hears what we say to them, and what enquiries we make upon them, and is much displeased if we pass them by without taking any notice of them. When we have heard the word we should apply to our ministers for further instruction; and then we shall know if we thus follow on to know. <div eID="gen18612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18613" type="x-p"/> 2. The prophet is to tell them the meaning of it. In general (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.10">v. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">This burden concerns the prince in Jerusalem;</hi> they knew who that was, and gloried in it now that they were in captivity that they had a prince of their own in Jerusalem, and that <hi type="italic">the house of Israel</hi> was yet entire there, and therefore doubted not but in time to do well enough. "But tell them," says God, "that in what thou hast done they may read the doom of their friends at Jerusalem. <hi type="italic">Say, I am your sign,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.11">v. 11</reference>. As the conversation of ministers should teach the people what they should do, so the providences of God concerning them are sometimes intended to tell them what they must expect. The unsettled state and removals of ministers give warning to people what they must expect in this world, no continuance, but constant changes. When times of trouble are coming on, Christ tells his disciples, <hi type="italic">They shall first lay their hands on you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.21.12">Luke xxi. 12</reference>. (1.) The people shall be led away into captivity (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">As I have done, so shall it be done unto them;</hi> they shall be forced away from their own houses, no more to return to them, neither shall <hi type="italic">their place know them any more.</hi> We cannot say concerning our dwelling-place that it is our resting-place; for how far we may be tossed from it before we die we cannot foresee. (2.) The prince shall in vain attempt to make his escape; for he also shall go into captivity. Jeremiah had told Zedekiah the same to his face (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.3">Jer. xxxiv. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not escape, but shalt surely be taken.</hi> Ezekiel here foretels it to those who made him their confidence and promised themselves relief from him. [1.] That he shall himself carry away his own goods: <hi type="italic">He shall bear upon his shoulder</hi> some of his most valuable effects. Note, The judgments of God can turn a prince into a porter. He that was wont to have the regalia carried before him, and to march through the city at noon-day, shall now himself carry his goods on his back and steal away out of the city in the twilight. See what a change sin makes with men! All the avenues to the palace being carefully watched by the enemy, <hi type="italic">they shall dig through the wall to carry out thereby.</hi> Men shall be their own house-breakers, and steal away their own goods; so it is when the sword of war has cancelled all right and property. [2.] That he shall attempt to escape in a disguise, with a mask or a visor on, which <hi type="italic">shall cover his face,</hi> so that he shall be able only to look before him, and shall <hi type="italic">not see the ground with his eyes.</hi> He who, when he was in pomp, affected to be seen, now that he is in his flight is afraid to be seen; let none therefore either be proud of being looked at or over-much pleased with looking about them, when they see a king with <hi type="italic">his face covered, that he cannot see the ground.</hi> [3.] That he shall be made a prisoner and carried captive into Babylon (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">My net will I spread upon him and he shall be taken in my snare.</hi> It seemed to be the Chaldeans' net and their snare, but God owns them for his. Those that think to escape the sword of the Lord will find themselves taken in his net. Jeremiah had said that king Zedekiah should <hi type="italic">see the king of Babylon</hi> and that he should <hi type="italic">go to Babylon;</hi> Ezekiel says, He shall be <hi type="italic">brought to Babylon,</hi> yet he <hi type="italic">shall not see it,</hi> though <hi type="italic">he shall die there.</hi> Those that were disposed to cavil would perhaps object that these two prophets contradicted one another; for one said, He shall <hi type="italic">see the king of Babylon,</hi> the other said, He shall <hi type="italic">not see Babylon;</hi> and yet both proved true: he did <hi type="italic">see the king of Babylon</hi> at Riblah, where he passed sentence upon him for his rebellion, but there he had his eyes put out, so that he did <hi type="italic">not see Babylon</hi> when he was brought thither. These captives expected to see their prince come to Babylon as a conqueror, to bring them out of their trouble; but he shall come thither a prisoner, and his disgrace will be a great addition to their troubles. Little joy could they have in seeing him when he could not see them. [4.] That all his guards should be dispersed and utterly disabled for doing him any service (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will scatter all that are about him to help him,</hi> so that he shall be left helpless; <hi type="italic">I will scatter them among the nations and disperse them in the countries</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.15">v. 15</reference>), to be monuments of divine justice wherever they go. But are there not hopes that they may rally again? (he that flies one time may fight another time); no: <hi type="italic">I will draw out the sword after them,</hi> which shall cut them off wherever if finds them; for the sword that God draws out will be sure to do the execution designed. Yet of Zedekiah's scattered troops some shall escape (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will leave a few men of them.</hi> Though they shall all be scattered, yet they shall not all be cut off; some shall have their <hi type="italic">lives given them for a prey.</hi> And the end for which they are thus remarkably spared is very observable: <hi type="italic">That they may declare all their abominations among the heathen whither they come;</hi> the troubles they are brought into will bring them to themselves and to their right mind, and then they will acknowledge the justice of God in all that is brought upon them and will make an ingenuous confession of their sins, which provoked God thus to contend with them; and, as by this it shall appear that they were spared in mercy, so hereby they will make a suitable grateful return to God for his favours to them in sparing them. Note, When God has remarkably delivered us from the deaths wherewith we were surrounded we must look upon it that for this end, among others, we were spared, that we might glorify God and edify others by making a penitent acknowledgment of our sins. Those that by their afflictions are brought to this are then made to know <hi type="italic">that God is the Lord</hi> and may help to bring others to the knowledge of him. See how God brings good out of evil. The dispersion of sinners, who had done God much dishonour and disservice in their own country, proves the dispersion of penitents, who shall do him much honour and service in others countries. The Levites are by a curse <hi type="italic">divided in Jacob</hi> and <hi type="italic">scattered in Israel,</hi> yet it is turned into a blessing, for thereby they have the fairest opportunity to <hi type="italic">teach Jacob God's laws.</hi>
entries.3bd597812b1de1fcf07851d070dc01b839925288: <div eID="gen18613" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Prediction of the Famine. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 593.)</title> <div sID="gen18614" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Moreover the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came to me, saying, <hi type="super">18</hi> Son of man, eat thy bread with quaking, and drink thy water with trembling and with carefulness; <hi type="super">19</hi> And say unto the people of the land, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">and</hi> of the land of Israel; They shall eat their bread with carefulness, and drink their water with astonishment, that her land may be desolate from all that is therein, because of the violence of all them that dwell therein. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the cities that are inhabited shall be laid waste, and the land shall be desolate; and ye shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen18614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18615" type="x-p"/> Here again the prophet is made a sign to them of the desolations that were coming on Judah and Jerusalem. 1. He must himself eat and drink in care and fear, especially when he was in company, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.17-Ezek.12.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. Though he was under no apprehension of danger to himself, but lived in safety and plenty, yet he must <hi type="italic">eat his bread with quaking</hi> (the bread of sorrows, <reference osisRef="Ps.127.2">Ps. cxxvii. 2</reference>) <hi type="italic">and drink his water with trembling and with carefulness,</hi> that he might express the calamitous condition of those that should be in Jerusalem during the siege; not that he must dissemble and pretend to be in fear and care when really he was not; but having to foretel this judgment, to show that he firmly believed it himself, and yet was far from desiring it, in the prospect of it he was himself affected with grief and fear. Note, When ministers speak of the ruin coming upon impenitent sinners they must endeavour to speak feelingly, as those that <hi type="italic">know the terrors of the Lord;</hi> and they must be content to endure hardness, so that they may but do good. 2. He must tell them that <hi type="italic">the inhabitants of Jerusalem</hi> should in like manner eat and drink with care and fear, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.19-Ezek.12.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. Both those that have their home in Jerusalem and those <hi type="italic">of the land of Israel</hi> that come to shelter themselves there, <hi type="italic">shall eat their bread with carefulness and drink their water with astonishment,</hi> either because they are afraid it will not hold out, but they shall want shortly, or because they are continually expecting the alarms of the enemy, <hi type="italic">their life hanging in doubt before them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.66">Deut. xxiii. 66</reference>), so that what they have they shall have no enjoyment of nor will it do them any good. Note, Care and fear, if they prevail, are enough to embitter all our comforts and are themselves very sore judgments. They shall be reduced to these straits that thus by degrees, and by the hand of those that thus straiten them, both city and country may be laid in ruins; for it is no less than an utter destruction of both that is aimed at in these judgments—<hi type="italic">that her land may be desolate from all</hi> the fulness thereof, may be stripped of all its ornaments and robbed of all its fruits, and then of course <hi type="italic">the cities that are inhabited shall be laid waste,</hi> for they are <hi type="italic">served by the field.</hi> This universal desolation was coming upon them, and then no wonder that they eat their bread with care and fear. Now we are here told, (1.) How bad the cause of this judgment was; it is <hi type="italic">because of the violence of all those that dwell therein,</hi> their injustice and oppression, and the mischief they did one another, for which God would reckon with them, as well as for the affronts put upon him in his worship. Note, The decay of virtue in a nation brings on a decay of every thing else; and when neighbours devour one another it is just with God to bring enemies upon them to devour them all. (2.) How good the effect of this judgment should be: <hi type="italic">You shall know that I am the Lord;</hi> and if, by these judgments, they learn to know him aright, that will make up the loss of all they are deprived of by these desolations. Those are happy afflictions, how grievous soever to flesh and blood, that help to introduce us into and improve us in an acquaintance with God.
entries.4a51b481c76b9d39220e70ae27354d0634515dd7: <div eID="gen18615" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Message from God to the People; Impious and Deceitful Hopes. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 593.)</title> <div sID="gen18616" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> And the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">22</hi> Son of man, what <hi type="italic">is</hi> that proverb <hi type="italic">that</hi> ye have in the land of Israel, saying, The days are prolonged, and every vision faileth? <hi type="super">23</hi> Tell them therefore, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; I will make this proverb to cease, and they shall no more use it as a proverb in Israel; but say unto them, The days are at hand, and the effect of every vision. <hi type="super">24</hi> For there shall be no more any vain vision nor flattering divination within the house of Israel. <hi type="super">25</hi> For I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : I will speak, and the word that I shall speak shall come to pass; it shall be no more prolonged: for in your days, O rebellious house, will I say the word, and will perform it, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">26</hi> Again the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came to me, saying, <hi type="super">27</hi> Son of man, behold, <hi type="italic">they of</hi> the house of Israel say, The vision that he seeth <hi type="italic">is</hi> for many days <hi type="italic">to come,</hi> and he prophesieth of the times <hi type="italic">that are</hi> far off. <hi type="super">28</hi> Therefore say unto them, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; There shall none of my words be prolonged any more, but the word which I have spoken shall be done, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen18616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18617" type="x-p"/> Various methods had been used to awaken this secure and careless people to an expectation of the judgments coming, that they might be stirred up, by repentance and reformation, to prevent them. The prophecies of their ruin were confirmed by visions, and illustrated by signs, and all with such evidence and power that one would think they must needs be wrought upon; but here we are told how they evaded the conviction, and guarded against it, namely, by telling themselves, and one another, that though these judgments threatened should come at last yet they would not come of a long time. This suggestion, with which they bolstered themselves up in their security, is here answered, and shown to be vain and groundless, in two separate messages which God sent to them by the prophet at different times, both to the same purport; such care, such pains, must the prophet take to undeceive them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.21">v. 21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.26">26</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen18617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18618" type="x-p"/> I. How they flattered themselves with hopes that the judgments should be delayed. One saying they had, which had become proverbial <hi type="italic">in the land of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.22">v. 22</reference>. They said, "<hi type="italic">The days are prolonged;</hi> the judgments have not come when they were expected to come, but seem to be still put off <hi type="italic">de die in diem—from day to day,</hi> and therefore we may conclude that <hi type="italic">every vision fails,</hi> because it should seem that some do, that because the destruction has not come yet it will never come; we will never trust a prophet again, for we have been more frightened than hurt." And another saying they had which, if it would not conquer their convictions, yet would cool their affections and abate their concern, and that was, "<hi type="italic">The vision</hi> is <hi type="italic">for</hi> a great while <hi type="italic">to come;</hi> it refers to events at a vast distance, <hi type="italic">and he prophesies of</hi> things which, though they may be true, are yet very <hi type="italic">far off,</hi> so that we need not trouble our heads about them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.27">v. 27</reference>); we may die in honour and peace before these troubles come." And, if indeed the troubles had been thus adjourned, they might have made themselves easy, as Hezekiah did. <hi type="italic">Is it not well if peace and truth shall be in my days?</hi> But it was a great mistake, and they did but deceive themselves into their own ruin; and God is here much displeased at it; for, 1. It was a wretched abuse of the patience of God, who, because for a time he kept silence, was thought to be <hi type="italic">altogether such a one as themselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.21">Ps. l. 21</reference>. That forbearance of God which should have led them to repentance hardened them in sin. They were willing to think their works were not <hi type="italic">evil because sentence against</hi> them was <hi type="italic">not executed speedily;</hi> and therefore concluded the <hi type="italic">vision</hi> itself <hi type="italic">failed,</hi> because <hi type="italic">the days were prolonged.</hi> 2. It received countenance from the false prophets that were among them, as should seem from the notice God takes (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.24">v. 24</reference>) of the <hi type="italic">vain visions,</hi> and <hi type="italic">flattering divinations,</hi> even <hi type="italic">within the house of Israel,</hi> to whom <hi type="italic">were committed the oracles of God.</hi> No marvel if those that deceived themselves by worshipping pretended deities deceived themselves also by crediting pretended prophecies, to which <hi type="italic">strong delusions</hi> God justly <hi type="italic">gave them up</hi> for their idolatries. 3. These sayings had become proverbial; they were industriously spread among the people, so that they had got into very one's mouth, and not only so, but were generally assented to, as proverbs usually are, not only the proverbs of the ancients, but those of the moderns too. Note, It is a token of universal degeneracy in a nation when corrupt and wicked sayings have grown proverbial; and it is an artifice of Satan by them to confirm men in their prejudices against the word and ways of God, and a great offence to the God of heaven. It will not serve for an excuse, in saying ill, to plead that it is a common saying. <div eID="gen18618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18619" type="x-p"/> II. How they are assured that they do but deceive themselves, for the judgments shall be hastened, these profane proverbs shall be confronted: <hi type="italic">Tell them, therefore, The days are at hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.23">v. 23</reference>), and again, <hi type="italic">There shall none of my words be prolonged any more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.28">v. 28</reference>. Their putting the evil day far from them does but provoke God to bring it the sooner upon them; and it will be so much the sorer, so much the heavier, so much the more a surprise and terror to them when it does come. He must tell them, <div eID="gen18619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18620" type="x-p"/> 1. That God will certainly silence the lying proverbs, and the lying prophecies, with which they buoyed up their vain hopes, and will make them ashamed of both: (1.) <hi type="italic">I will make this proverb to cease;</hi> for when they find the days of vengeance have come, and not one iota or tittle of the prediction falls to the ground, they will be ashamed to <hi type="italic">use it as a proverb in Israel, The days are prolonged, and the vision fails.</hi> Note, Those that will not have their eyes opened and their mistakes rectified, by the word of God, shall be undeceived by his judgments: for <hi type="italic">every mouth</hi> that speaks perverse things <hi type="italic">shall be stopped.</hi> (2.) <hi type="italic">There shall be no more any vain vision,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.24">v. 24</reference>. The false prophets, who told the people they should have peace and should soon see an end of their troubles, shall be disproved by the event, and then shall be ashamed of their pretensions, and shall hide their heads and impose silence upon themselves. Note, As truth was older than error, so it will survive it; it got the start, and it will get the race. The true prophets' visions and predictions stand, and are in full force, power, and virtue; they give law, and receive credit, when the <hi type="italic">vain visions,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">flattering divinations,</hi> are lost and forgotten, and <hi type="italic">shall be no more in the house of Israel;</hi> for <hi type="italic">great is the truth, and will prevail.</hi> <div eID="gen18620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18621" type="x-p"/> 2. That God will certainly, and very shortly, accomplish every word that he has spoken. With what majesty does he say it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.25">v. 25</reference>): I <hi type="italic">am the</hi> <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ! <hi type="italic">I am Jehovah!</hi> That glorious name of his speaks him a God giving being to his word by the performance of it, and therefore to the patriarchs, who lived by faith in a promise not yet performed, he was not known by his name <hi type="italic">Jehovah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.6.3">Exod. vi. 3</reference>. But, as he is Jehovah in making good his promise, so he is in making good his threatenings. Let them know then that God, <hi type="italic">with whom they have to do,</hi> is the great Jehovah, and therefore, (1.) He will speak, <hi type="italic">whether they will hear or whether they will forbear: I am the Lord, I will speak.</hi> God will have his saying, whoever gainsays it. God's oracles are called <hi type="italic">lively</hi> ones, for they still speak when the pagan oracles are long ago struck dumb. There has been, and shall be, a succession of God's ministers to the end of the world, by whom he will speak; and, though contempt may be put upon them, that shall not put a period to their ministration: <hi type="italic">In your days, O rebellious house! will I say the word.</hi> Even in the worst ages of the church God <hi type="italic">left not himself without witness,</hi> but raised up men that spoke for him, that spoke from him. <hi type="italic">I will say the word,</hi> the word that shall stand. (2.) The word that he speaks shall come to pass; it shall infallibly be accomplished according to the true intent and meaning of it, and according to the full extent and compass of it: <hi type="italic">I will say the word and will perform it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.25">v. 25</reference>), for his mind is never changed, nor his arm shortened, nor is Infinite Wisdom ever nonplussed. With men saying and doing are two things, but they are not so with God; with him it is <hi type="italic">dictum, factum—said, and done.</hi> In the works of providence, as in those of creation, <hi type="italic">he speaks and it is done;</hi> for he said, <hi type="italic">Let there be light, and there was light—Let there be a firmament, and there was a firmament,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.23.19">Num. xxiii. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.29">1 Sam. xv. 29</reference>. Whereas they had said, <hi type="italic">Every vision fails</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.22">v. 22</reference>), God says, "No, there shall be <hi type="italic">the effect of every vision</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.23">v. 23</reference>); it shall not return void, but every sign shall be answered by the thing signified." Those that <hi type="italic">see the visions of the Almighty</hi> do not see <hi type="italic">vain visions;</hi> God <hi type="italic">confirms the word of his servants</hi> by performing it. (3.) It shall be accomplished very shortly: "<hi type="italic">The days are at hand</hi> when you shall see <hi type="italic">the effect of every vision,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.23">v. 23</reference>. It is said, it is sworn, that delay <hi type="italic">shall be no longer</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.10.6">Rev. x. 6</reference>); the year of God's patience has now just expired, and he will no longer defer the execution of the sentence. <hi type="italic">It shall be no more prolonged</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.25">v. 25</reference>); he has borne with you a great while, but he will not bear always. <hi type="italic">In your days, O rebellious house!</hi> shall the word that is said be <hi type="italic">performed,</hi> and you shall see the threatened judgments and share in them. <hi type="italic">Behold, the Judge stands at the door.</hi> The <hi type="italic">righteous are taken away from the evil to come,</hi> but this <hi type="italic">rebellious house</hi> shall not be so quietly taken away; no, they shall live to be hurried away, to <hi type="italic">be chased out of the world.</hi>" This is repeated (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.28">v. 28</reference>): "<hi type="italic">There shall none of my words be prolonged any more,</hi> but judgment shall now hasten on apace; and the longer the bow has been in the drawing the deeper shall the arrow pierce." When we tell sinners of death and judgment, heaven and hell, and think by them to persuade them to a holy life, though we do not find them downright infidels (they will own that they do believe there is a state of rewards and punishments in the other world), yet they put by the force of those great truths, and void the impressions of them, by looking upon the things of the other world as very remote; they tell us, "<hi type="italic">The vision</hi> you <hi type="italic">see is for many days to come, and</hi> you <hi type="italic">prophesy of the times that are</hi> very <hi type="italic">far off;</hi> it will be time enough to think of them when they come nearer," whereas really there is but a step between us and death, between us and an awful eternity; <hi type="italic">yet a little while and the vision shall speak and not lie,</hi> and therefore it concerns us to redeem time, and get ready with all speed for a future state; for, though it is future, it is very near, and while impenitent sinners slumber their <hi type="italic">damnation slumbers not.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ezek.12"/> <div eID="gen18621" type="x-p"/>

entries.c02132a1e67eeb7c3ba634602ded9f9815b847d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11139"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 12</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.12.1-Ezek.12.28">Eze 12:1-28</reference>. Ezekiel's Typical Moving to Exile: Prophecy of Zedekiah's Captivity and Privation of Sight: the Jews' Unbelieving Surmise as to the Distance of the Event Reproved.</title> <div sID="gen20079" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11139"/><hi type="bold">1-2. eyes to see, and see not, ... ears to hear, and hear not--</hi>fulfilling the prophecy of <reference osisRef="Deut.29.4">De 29:4</reference>, here quoted by Ezekiel (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.6.9">Is 6:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.21">Jr 5:21</reference>). Ezekiel needed often to be reminded of the people's perversity, lest he should be discouraged by the little effect produced by his prophecies. Their "not seeing" is the result of perversity, not incapacity. They are wilfully blind. The persons most interested in this prophecy were those dwelling at Jerusalem; and it is among them that Ezekiel was transported in spirit, and performed in vision, not outwardly, the typical acts. At the same time, the symbolical prophecy was designed to warn the exiles at Chebar against cherishing hopes, as many did in opposition to God's revealed word, of returning to Jerusalem, as if that city was to stand; externally living afar off, their hearts dwelt in that corrupt and doomed capital. <div eID="gen20079" type="x-p"/>
entries.03c63526a24a03eb170f7447932c5856e9478bfe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11140"/><div sID="gen20080" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11140"/><hi type="bold">3. stuff for removing--</hi>rather, "an exile's outfit," the articles proper to a person going as an exile, a staff and knapsack, with a supply of food and clothing; so "instruments of captivity," <reference osisRef="Jer.46.19">Jr 46:19</reference>, Margin, that is, the needful equipments for it. His simple announcements having failed, he is symbolically to give them an ocular demonstration conveyed by a word-painting of actions performed in vision.<div eID="gen20080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">consider--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.32.29">De 32:29</reference>). <div eID="gen20081" type="x-p"/>
entries.e71b6ba3991ebcd05acbceabbdf577de062c9b33: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11141"/><div sID="gen20082" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11141"/><hi type="bold">4. by day--</hi>in broad daylight, when all can see thee.<div eID="gen20082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20083" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at even--</hi>not contradicting the words "by day." The baggage was to be sent before by day, and Ezekiel was to follow at nightfall [Grotius]; or, the preparations were to be made by day, the actual departure was to be effected at night [Henderson].<div eID="gen20083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20084" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as they that go forth into captivity--</hi>literally, "as the goings forth of the captivity," that is, of the captive band of exiles, namely, amid the silent darkness: typifying Zedekiah's flight by night on the taking of the city (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.4">Jr 39:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.7">52:7</reference>). <div eID="gen20084" type="x-p"/>

entries.f0e1430f9502186313b0f8a7bfbed712320e1a70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11145"/><div sID="gen20092" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11145"/><hi type="bold">10. burden--</hi>that is, weighty oracle.<div eID="gen20092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the prince--</hi>The very man Zedekiah, in whom they trust for safety, is to be the chief sufferer. Josephus [Antiquities, 10.7] reports that Ezekiel sent a copy of this prophecy to Zedekiah. As Jeremiah had sent a letter to the captives at the Chebar, which was the means of calling forth at first the agency of Ezekiel, so it was natural for Ezekiel to send a message to Jerusalem confirming the warnings of Jeremiah. The prince, however, fancying a contradiction between <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>; "he shall not see Babylon," and <reference osisRef="Jer.24.8">Jr 24:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.24.9">9</reference>, declaring he should be carried to Babylon, believed neither. Seeming discrepancies in Scripture on deeper search prove to be hidden harmonies. <div eID="gen20093" type="x-p"/>

entries.cbfb9b47a4880118d726226e85418150524a23b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11147"/><div sID="gen20095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11147"/><hi type="bold">12. prince ... among them--</hi>literally, "that is in the midst of them," that is, on whom the eyes of all are cast, and "under whose shadow" they hope to live (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.20">La 4:20</reference>).<div eID="gen20095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20096" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall bear--</hi>namely, his "stuff for removing"; his equipments for his journey.<div eID="gen20096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20097" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cover his face, that he see not the ground--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.6">Eze 12:6</reference>; the symbol in <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.6">Eze 12:6</reference> is explained in this verse. He shall muffle his face so as not to be recognized: a humiliation for a king! <div eID="gen20097" type="x-p"/>

entries.f91c8ddcea2d0c749c967a5638e79e977051ece0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11149"/><div sID="gen20100" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11149"/><hi type="bold">14. all ... about him--</hi>his satellites: his bodyguard.<div eID="gen20100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20101" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bands--</hi>literally, "the wings" of an army (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">Is 8:8</reference>).<div eID="gen20101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">draw out ... sword after them--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.2">Eze 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.12">Eze 5:12</reference>). <div eID="gen20102" type="x-p"/>
entries.8bba2cc027a0c037dd00eed72b28fcf8288f311f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11150"/><div sID="gen20103" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11150"/><hi type="bold">16. I will leave a few ... that they may declare ... abominations--</hi>God's purpose in scattering a remnant of Jews among the Gentiles; namely, not only that they themselves should be weaned from idolatry (see <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.15">Eze 12:15</reference>), but that by their own word, as also by their whole state as exiles, they should make God's righteousness manifest among the Gentiles, as vindicated in their punishment for their sins (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.43.10">Is 43:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.8.13">Zec 8:13</reference>). <div eID="gen20103" type="x-p"/>
